questions.q: Why does the blog schema in this lesson reference the post's author (`authorId`) instead of embedding the author's full profile?
options: A user writes many posts, and their profile changes independently — embedding would mean updating every copy on every profile edit
MongoDB doesn't allow embedding user data under any circumstances
References are always faster than embedding, with no tradeoffs
Author profiles are too small to be embedded
questions.explain: This is the one-to-many, changes-independently case Lesson 8 flagged as a referencing fit — exactly why authorId is a reference, not an embed.

questions.q: Why does the blog schema embed comments directly inside the post document (for a normal, non-viral post)?
options: Comments are read essentially every time the post is read, so embedding avoids a second query for data that's almost always needed together
MongoDB requires all child data to be embedded
Comments never change once written, so embedding is the only safe option
Embedding is required for any array field
questions.explain: Data read together almost every time is the strongest embedding signal — nobody loads a blog post without its comment thread.

questions.q: What operator does this lesson use to add a new comment to an embedded `comments` array?
options: $push
$set
$pull
$insert
questions.explain: $push appends a value to an array field — used here to add a new embedded comment atomically.

questions.q: What real problem occurs when a post's embedded comments array grows very large (e.g. a viral post)?
options: It approaches the 16MB BSON document size limit, and every read of the post drags the whole growing array along with it
MongoDB automatically deletes older comments once the array is full
The post document becomes read-only
MongoDB silently splits the document across multiple servers with no code changes needed
questions.explain: The same 16MB document ceiling and unbounded-growth concern from Lesson 8 apply — and reads get slower well before that hard limit.

questions.q: What is the 'hybrid pattern' this lesson describes as the fix for a viral post's comments?
options: Keep a small number of recent comments embedded for fast normal reads, and move the full comment history to its own collection referenced by postId
Delete all comments once a threshold is crossed
Convert the post document into a graph node
Store all comments in a separate database entirely disconnected from posts
questions.explain: The hybrid pattern embeds a bounded subset for the common case while referencing the full set elsewhere — mixing both patterns within one relationship.
